title: My Journey With Building My Own Site With React
excerpt: From knowing almost nothing about React to building this personal website from scratch — the bugs, the struggles, and what I actually learned.
content:
When I first decided to build this website, I had one major problem — I barely knew React. I had mostly worked with vanilla JavaScript, some jQuery, and a lot of plain CSS. React felt like an entirely different beast.

The first week was pure pain. I spent hours just trying to understand why my components were not re-rendering, why state was not updating, and why the hell my CSS was breaking every time I made a small change. The famous 'Cannot read properties of undefined' error became my worst enemy.

What made it worse was that I was not following any proper structure. I was writing everything inside one giant component. My About section had become a monster with 300+ lines of code. That's when I realised — I was doing everything wrong.

Slowly I started breaking things down. I created separate components for Header, About, Projects, and Blog. I learned the importance of lifting state up, how to properly manage props, and why everyone keeps screaming about 'separation of concerns'.

One of the biggest challenges was making this website responsive. What looked perfect on my laptop looked like a complete disaster on mobile. Fixing the grid layouts, making the experience cards look good on small screens, and ensuring the blog cards didn't break the layout took me countless hours.

The design decisions were equally painful. Should I go with a dark theme? Should I use Tailwind or stick with plain CSS? I tried both and eventually realised that for a personal website, clean design with good typography matters more than flashy animations.

The most satisfying moment was when I finally got the About section right — with the experience cards, proper spacing, and that clean blue accent. It was the first time the website actually started to feel like 'me'.

This project taught me much more than just React. It taught me how to debug properly, how to break down complex UIs into smaller components, the importance of planning before coding, and most importantly — how to keep pushing even when nothing seems to work.

If you're also learning React and feeling overwhelmed, just know that it's completely normal. The struggle is part of the process. Keep building. Keep breaking things. And most importantly, keep shipping.

This website is not perfect. There are still many things I want to improve. But it's mine. I built it from scratch with my own hands, one frustrating bug at a time.

And that feeling — there's nothing quite like it.

title: The Paradox of the Absolute: Why Creation Might Be Necessary
excerpt: If the Absolute or God is already complete and self-sufficient, why does the universe exist? A personal exploration of a deep tension in Advaita Vedanta and classical philosophy.
content:
For a long time, I have been thinking about one of the deepest questions in philosophy: Why did the Absolute or God create the universe?

In Advaita Vedanta, the standard answer is that Brahman is purna — complete and self-sufficient. Creation is just lila, spontaneous divine play, without any purpose or necessity. The Absolute didn't need to create anything. It just happened.

But the more I think about it, the more this explanation feels incomplete.

Here are the strongest points that trouble me:

1. Spontaneous Lila Creates a Contradiction

If the Absolute is truly omniscient and the source of everything, how can anything be truly "spontaneous" or without intent?

True spontaneity implies something happening outside of will or knowledge. But if the Absolute is all-knowing, nothing can fall outside its knowledge. Calling creation "spontaneous lila" seems like a convenient way to avoid the question rather than answering it.

2. Relational Attributes Require Manifestation

Many attributes we traditionally give to the Absolute — such as omniscience regarding time, causality, and change — are relational.

Time is not a static thing that can be known in pure abstraction. It is a process. Causality is a relationship between events. These things only make sense inside a manifested universe. How can the Absolute fully possess these attributes in a state of pure, non-dual oneness where no time or change exists?

3. The Distinction Between Potential and Actualization

There is a fundamental difference between possessing infinite potential and actualizing it.

The Absolute may know itself completely and possess infinite creative potential. But knowing you can run is not the same as running. An unexercised potential is, in a meaningful sense, not fully real. Creation may be the necessary medium through which the Absolute moves from potential to actuality.

The very existence of this vast, complex, and finely balanced universe suggests that creation is not optional play, but serves a real function for the Absolute.

This is not a final conclusion. It is an honest exploration. The classical explanations feel too clean, too convenient. They seem to avoid the deep tension between "the Absolute is complete" and "the universe exists."

I believe this paradox deserves to be examined more seriously, without rushing to say "it is inexplicable" or "it is just play."

What do you think? Is creation necessary for the Absolute to fully express its nature, or is the traditional view correct?
